macro-week-2026-07-26:
Four numbers landed within days of each other this week, and they pull in different directions at once. China's central bank pumped $118.1 billion combined into its banking system through medium-term loans and reverse repos, the most since February, right after weak growth data. Chinese buyers imported 173 tonnes of gold in June, the most in a single month since March 2024. Meanwhile in the United States, investors pulled $7.1 billion out of investment-grade corporate bond funds in a week, the fastest outflow since the pandemic. And globally, emerging-market carry trades, borrowing in euros to chase yield in currencies like the Brazilian real and Turkish lira, are up 18% this year, their best start since 2005.

Read side by side, these don't tell one story, they tell two that pull against each other. Gold buying and central bank liquidity injections are defensive moves, the kind a government makes when it doesn't fully trust its own growth numbers. Carry trades are the opposite: money chasing yield with borrowed cash, a bet that calm currency markets keep paying out. Sitting in between is the corporate bond outflow, quiet stress in US credit that isn't showing up in stock prices or currency volatility yet.

## How to read four signals pointing in different directions
Put together, the picture is a market that is barbelling risk. Currency traders are leaning further into risk-taking than they have in two decades, while China hedges its own growth doubts with gold and stimulus, and US credit investors quietly step back from corporate debt. None of these four moves cancels out the others, they are happening at the same time, in different corners of the same global market.
meru-china-russia-gas-talks-collapse:
Gas pricing negotiations between Russia and China over the second Power of Siberia (POS2) pipeline have collapsed.
China reportedly offered $50 per 1,000 cubic meters; Russia asked for $250, according to Korean market commentator Meru.

The numbers check out. Asia Times and bne IntelliNews both independently confirm China's $50 offer and Russia's $250 ask.
Russia's own delivery cost from its Yamal fields to China runs around $125 per 1,000 cubic meters.
China currently pays $240-280 through the existing Power of Siberia 1 line. Gazprom charges other
international buyers an average of around $420, and China's LNG import price runs around $370.
Against those numbers, China's $50 doesn't even cover Russia's delivery cost, while Russia's $250 ask
looks like a reasonable middle ground.

@@REF@@Power of Siberia 2 deadlock belies Russia-China 'no-limits' pact (Asia Times, 2026-07-16)|https://asiatimes.com/2026/07/power-of-siberia-2-deadlock-cracks-russia-china-no-limits-pact/|https://asiatimes.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Xi_Putin.jpg

## Meru points to a bridge dispute as the reason
Meru links the breakdown to an entirely different dispute: a rail bridge over the Tumen River, on the
China-North Korea border. Completed in April 2026, the bridge could give China access to the Sea of
Japan, but Russia's side has been slow finishing approach roads and customs facilities, and North Korea
reportedly suspects Russia is deliberately dragging its feet out of deference to China. Meru's theory
is that China's unusually low gas offer could be a signal of frustration over the bridge.

@@REF@@Tumen River bridge delay rattles North Korea (Daily NK, 2026-06-24)|https://www.dailynk.com/english/tumen-river-bridge-delay-north-korea-russia/|https://www.dailynk.com/english/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/06/tumen-river-north-korea-russia-china-border-fangchuan.jpg

The bridge dispute itself is real and independently reported. But no wire service or outlet, including
this one, connects the bridge to the gas talks. Meru himself is careful to add that China's real motive
can't be confirmed from outside.

@@CMP@@Meru's read|China's unusually low offer could be a signal of frustration or retaliation over the delayed bridge.|What other sources suggest|POS2 is still pre-construction and China is Russia's only realistic large buyer, so the lowball may just be a negotiating tactic from the side that isn't in a hurry.
The split is whether the price gap is a political message, or simply a calculation from the side with nothing to lose by waiting.

## The real leverage looks like it's somewhere else
Analysis from the Carnegie Endowment shows POS2 is still stuck at a September 2025 agreement-in-principle
stage, with construction likely taking at least five years and gas flows not expected before 2031.
Both sides are negotiating over a pipeline that still exists only on paper.

Over the same period, Russia's pipeline gas exports to Europe fell 44% in 2025 alone, hitting their
lowest level since the mid-1970s. The Ukraine transit route shut down in January 2025, leaving only
TurkStream. In Carnegie's own words, "China is the only buyer capable of taking the huge quantity of
gas [Russia] has available."

@@REF@@Russia's Pipeline Gas Sales to Europe Plunge to 50-Year Low (OilPrice.com, 2025-12-30)|https://oilprice.com/Energy/Natural-Gas/Russias-Pipeline-Gas-Sales-to-Europe-Plunge-to-50-Year-Low.html

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The question comes down to one thing: is China's $50 offer a political signal tied to the bridge,
or just hardball from the side under no time pressure?

If it's really a political message, watch whether the bridge's approach-road construction suddenly
speeds up, or keeps dragging. If it's pure commercial leverage, expect construction to keep slipping
while China announces new LNG contracts elsewhere first.

A pipeline can't be rerouted to another buyer once it's built. Time isn't on Russia's side, and China
has no reason to be in a hurry yet.
jukan-goldman-china-dram-catchup:
Goldman Sachs held an expert call with a Chinese DRAM industry insider, and semiconductor analyst Jukan relayed the key takeaways. The headline point: Chinese DRAM makers' prices have already caught up to global leaders like Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron.

## How close has it actually gotten
A direct comparison by Tom's Hardware on July 26 found CXMT's 64GB DDR5-5600 RDIMM selling for 18,999 yuan on JD.com, versus 18,595 yuan for equivalent Samsung/SK hynix modules, a gap of just 2.2%. SemiAnalysis separately found CXMT's Q1 2026 average selling prices had narrowed to within 5-10% of the big three, and that the quarter's earnings improvement came mainly from pricing (up roughly 57% quarter over quarter), not volume growth.

@@REF@@Chinese CXMT DRAM doesn't look like the budget savior many were expecting (Tom's Hardware, 2026-07-26)|https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/dram/chinese-cxmt-dram-doesnt-look-like-the-budget-savior-many-were-expecting-new-modules-enter-the-market-but-prices-still-track-the-big-three|https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/Y6RXNGdt5atPtqKHjD7EUW-1280-80.jpg

## The catch: this parity is mainstream-only
Per memory vendors WCCFTech spoke to at Computex in June, this price convergence is limited to entry-level and mainstream DDR5 modules running up to 8000 MT/s. CXMT has essentially no presence in premium formats like CUDIMM, CQDIMM or MRDIMM. So "Chinese DRAM matches Samsung" is true for a slice of the lineup, not the whole thing.

"Yield" is the share of chips on a wafer that come out working. SemiAnalysis estimates CXMT's cost per bit runs more than 30% above the big three, partly because its die is around 40% larger than Samsung's, meaning fewer working chips per wafer. Charging within 2% of leader prices while carrying that much higher cost points to either eating losses to defend share, or state subsidies covering the gap. No report found actually documents subsidies covering that specific price gap, though. What is documented is capex-stage support, like a Hefei state investment vehicle funding around 80% of CXMT's Phase 1 buildout.

@@REF@@China's CXMT Is Set to Challenge DRAM Incumbents (SemiAnalysis, 2026-06-23)|https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/chinas-cxmt-is-set-to-challenge-dram

## The bigger story may be industry-wide, not subsidy-driven
A larger reason prices have converged: Samsung, SK hynix and Micron have been redirecting wafer capacity toward AI-driven HBM, tightening the overall supply of conventional DRAM industry-wide. CXMT has no HBM pivot to make, so it kept its volume relatively intact. This looks less like CXMT winning on price and more like its rivals stepping out of the way.

A technology roadmap came up too. Chinese DRAM makers are expected to make further progress on 3D-stacked DRAM in 2027, and capacity expansions in Hefei, Shanghai and Beijing are slated to be fully operational by 2028.

## Is blocking lithography alone enough
Some fabs reportedly run mostly on domestically produced Chinese equipment, with one exception: high-end lithography, the machines that etch circuit patterns onto wafers. But that chokepoint isn't just EUV. Tom's Hardware reports China began delivering domestically made immersion DUV (ArFi) tools to SMIC, Hua Hong and CXMT in 2026, though commercial-scale self-sufficiency isn't expected until the mid-2030s. ASML still holds 98.7% of the immersion DUV market.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The question comes down to one thing: is Chinese DRAM matching leader prices despite lower yields a loss-leading share defense, subsidy power, or simply a windfall from the industry's own pivot to HBM.

Once Samsung, SK hynix and Micron dial back HBM and return to conventional DRAM, CXMT's pricing power gets tested for real. If the gap stays around 2%, China's catch-up is real. If it widens again, this "price parity" will have been a temporary window opened by the industry's own capacity shift.
jukan-huawei-ai-chip-shipments-double:
Huawei is on track to ship around 1.5 million of its own AI accelerator chips this year, roughly double the volume it shipped in 2025, according to a Wall Street Journal report relayed by semiconductor analyst Jukan on X. The jump matters because it comes despite years of US export controls designed to cut China off from advanced chipmaking equipment and Nvidia's most powerful GPUs.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/NVIDIA_GPU.jpg/960px-NVIDIA_GPU.jpg|An AI accelerator chip. Huawei's Ascend line plugs into data center servers in a similar form factor.|Wikimedia Commons|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NVIDIA_GPU.jpg

## The exact 1.5 million figure doesn't hold up under scrutiny
The original WSJ article sits behind a paywall and couldn't be verified directly. Other outlets' own shipment estimates, gathered together, tell a messier story. Bloomberg put 2025 Ascend 910C shipments at roughly 300,000 units (up to 1 million dies across the whole Ascend line) and 2026 at 600,000 units (up to 1.6 million dies). SemiAnalysis put actual 2025 shipments at 805,000 units (653,000 of them 910C). JPMorgan, cited by Tom's Hardware, put SMIC-based output at 600,000-650,000 in 2025 and 800,000-850,000 in 2026. The US Commerce Department separately estimated Huawei's 2025 capacity at under 200,000 units, three to seven times lower than the industry estimates above. No single source independently confirms "exactly 1.5 million, exactly double."

@@REF@@China's chip champions ramp up production of AI accelerators at domestic fabs, but HBM and fab production capacity are towering bottlenecks (Tom's Hardware, 2025-09-10)|https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/chinas-chip-champions-ramp-up-production-of-ai-accelerators-at-domestic-fabs-but-hbm-and-fab-production-capacity-are-towering-bottlenecks|https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/yhFcLNWMWBru4ox6DxUvQG-2560-80.jpg

## The real bottleneck isn't lithography, it's HBM
Huawei's AI chips sell under the Ascend brand, and export controls first imposed in 2019 and tightened since have blocked Huawei from buying the most advanced lithography tools or importing Nvidia's top chips. But SemiAnalysis and Tom's Hardware independently point to a different constraint as the real one: high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Huawei's pre-restriction HBM stockpile, estimated at around 11.7 million stacks, was expected to run out by the end of 2025, and domestic substitute CXMT's annual capacity of roughly 2.2 million stacks supports only 250,000-400,000 910C packages. A July 2026 Bloomberg Intelligence survey still named HBM shortage as the biggest bottleneck.

@@CMP@@Common read|Export controls have starved China of AI compute, keeping it years behind.|What multiple analysts show|The real constraint on Huawei isn't lithography, it's the pre-restriction HBM stockpile running dry, and once it does, shipments could fall well short of 1.5 million.
Inside the same export-control story, analysts disagree on which specific component is actually doing the choking.

DigiTimes reported Huawei's SMIC-made 7nm-class chip yield rising from around 20% in September 2024 to around 40% in early 2025, but no updated figure beyond that could be found. That's still well below TSMC's 90%-plus yields at comparable nodes.

## Who's actually buying this volume
ByteDance reportedly planned around $5.6 billion in Ascend chip orders in December 2025, and a March 2026 Reuters report relayed by CNBC said ByteDance and Alibaba were considering orders for the newer, inference-focused Ascend 950PR. That suggests a meaningful share of what's shipping now is going to inference workloads, not frontier model training.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The question comes down to one thing: is Huawei's shipment jump proof that export controls failed to contain China's AI chips, or a number propped up by stockpiled memory that's about to run out.

If Huawei's HBM stockpile actually empties by the end of 2025 and shipments keep climbing anyway, that's real self-sufficiency. If shipments stall right around then, this "doubling" report will have been a one-time number borrowed from inventory that's already spent.
jukan-nand-sandisk-lta-bearish-pushback:
## What actually got sold cheap
NAND holds the photos on your phone and the files on your laptop.
It keeps them with the power off,
and Meta stacks it in data centres.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/USB_flash_drive.JPG/500px-USB_flash_drive.JPG|The USB stick in your drawer. The storage chip inside it is NAND.|Wikimedia Commons|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:USB_flash_drive.JPG

NAND types differ by bits per storage cell.
TLC holds three, QLC holds four.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Cell_types_SLC-PLC_in_comparison_20211102.svg/1280px-Cell_types_SLC-PLC_in_comparison_20211102.svg.png|Bits per cell, side by side. Third from the left is TLC, fourth is QLC.|Wikimedia Commons|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cell_types_SLC-PLC_in_comparison_20211102.svg

More bits per cell means more storage per area, so unit cost falls.
The cell also wears faster and runs slower.

QLC is the cheap end, TLC the durable one.
QLC is the one in question.

## Why sign below the going rate
A long-term agreement, or LTA, fixes volume and price years ahead.

Think of it as a phone contract.
Lock in for two years, the monthly bill drops.
The buyer promises volume, the seller shaves the price.
The fab stays busy, so both sides want it.

An LTA below the spot rate is the normal outcome, not a warning.
SanDisk plans to fill over half its shipments this way, which tilts it further.

## So is $0.38 actually cheap
SanDisk opened near $0.50 a unit, expensive for QLC and close to TLC money.

The deal settled near $0.38, a 24% cut.
@@REF@@SanDisk secures Meta NAND supply deal (Yahoo Finance, 2026-07-24)|https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/sandisk-sndk-secures-meta-nand-171417598.html|https://media.zenfs.com/en/simply_wall_st__316/4ede54afa2108a12bdee07c0b0d94a59

@@CMP@@The bear read|A 24% cut from $0.50 to $0.38. You do not discount that hard on something that sells itself.|Jukan's read|$0.50 was TLC money to begin with. $0.38 is closer to fair, and the LTA took the rest.

Same number, opposite readings, depending on where you set the baseline.

## Is the China story a demand signal
One more story props up the bear case, from China.

Module makers there were reportedly turned away selling enterprise SSDs at home.
A module maker buys NAND chips and assembles them into drives.
@@REF@@Chinese memory vendors pick homegrown YMTC and CXMT over Samsung and Micron (Tom's Hardware, 2026-06-17)|https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/ram/chinese-memory-vendors-snub-industry-giants-in-favor-of-homegrown-ram-chips-samsung-micron-and-sk-hynix-face-a-chinese-supply-chain-revolt|https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/tn9gFjhWREg7FV67sMTNJY-2560-80.jpg

Jukan places the cause elsewhere.
Those clouds already buy direct from YMTC, China's own NAND maker.

No reason for a middleman differs from nothing to buy.

## Is an LTA only a safe card
Jukan treats SanDisk filling half its shipments with LTAs as a bull point.
Turn it over and it becomes a cost.

With half the volume fixed years out,
a rise in NAND prices cannot reach it.

An LTA is a floor when prices fall and a ceiling when they climb.
The more bullish on memory, the less appealing a company that pre-sold half its output.

The spread of LTAs is also hard to read as weakness.
Intel and AMD are reportedly signing CPU LTAs with Chinese customers.

Ibiden is the Japanese maker of substrates that package advanced chips.
When Samsung sought them,
Ibiden reportedly asked for LTA guarantees.

That is the buyer locking supply down.
@@REF@@Intel and AMD to sign CPU LTAs with Chinese customers (Serenity, 2026-07-23)|https://x.com/aleabitoreddit/status/2080153334888182065

## What the next two days did
Two days later the market moved the other way.

On the 27th SanDisk fell over 14% in a session,
47% below its June 22 high.
About $170 billion of market value went in a month.

None of that proves Jukan wrong on how the contract was priced.
It does say the market reads this as the cycle, not the contract.
@@REF@@SanDisk drops 14% in a day, 47% off its June high (The Kobeissi Letter, 2026-07-27)|https://x.com/KobeissiLetter/status/2081814364928057486

## What settles it
The question comes down to one thing.
Did the discount come from the contract, or from the cycle turning?
If it is the contract, this drop can reverse.
If it is the cycle, it has further to run.

Two things will tell.

If next quarter's QLC contract prints above $0.38, Jukan's read holds.
If below, $0.38 was a starting point, not a floor.

And if SanDisk's LTA share clears half,
there will be a stretch where NAND rises and this name lags.

Either way, a company with half its volume at fixed prices
rises less on the way up and sinks less on the way down.
That asymmetry comes before the direction call.
jukan-cxmt-3d-ic-niche-strategy:
The chip industry's race to boost AI performance is shifting from process shrinks to 3D stacking, which fuses logic and memory in one package, and Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are staying cautious about commercializing it while China's ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) moves to claim the niche, semiconductor analyst Jukan reports.

## What actually separates 3D IC from HBM
HBM stacks DRAM on a base logic die that mostly handles input/output and signal routing, then connects to a separate compute chip through an interposer, essentially a standardized off-the-shelf product. "True" 3D IC, or memory-on-logic, uses hybrid bonding and through-silicon vias to attach DRAM directly onto the compute logic die itself, eliminating the interposer and shortening data paths. Reported gains run around 22% performance and 36% power, but it comes with a thermal mismatch between DRAM (tolerant to roughly 80°C) and logic (120-125°C), tricky bonding yields, and, crucially, a design that's specific to each customer rather than a standard catalog part.

## CXMT's 3D IC push is a workaround, not pure innovation
CXMT is blocked from the HBM market outright by US export controls. TSMC controls roughly 90% of global CoWoS packaging capacity and won't service leading Chinese AI firms, and HBM-specific manufacturing and packaging tools were added to export controls in December 2024. CXMT's 3D IC move reads more like "can't grow in HBM, so open a different niche instead." CXMT is reportedly already ahead of rivals in producing several 3D DRAM sample chips, though that "ahead" claim is specifically a comparison against Korea's Samsung and SK hynix, not a verified claim against the whole world including Micron or Winbond.

@@REF@@China's CXMT Is Betting On Customized DRAM To Circumvent U.S. Sanctions On HBM (wccftech, 2026-07-24)|https://wccftech.com/cxmt-custom-dram-us-sanctions-hbm/|https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/CXMT-3.jpg

## The real reason Samsung and SK hynix are cautious
Industry officials say custom, 3D-stacked DRAM is a fundamentally different business from the standardized, mass-produced DRAM that Samsung and SK hynix are built around, since every customer wants a different memory configuration and stacking method, making it hard to run profitably at scale.

But that's not the whole story. TrendForce reports Samsung is planning a 50% HBM capacity surge in 2026, and SK hynix is aiming to double its DRAM capacity in the second half of 2026 to catch up with Samsung. Both companies' capex and engineering headcount are already fully mobilized around expanding HBM4 and HBM4E. It's less that they're refusing 3D IC and more that they have no spare bandwidth for it right now. Samsung is in fact building a hybrid-bonding mass-production line at Pyeongtaek, but full-scale deployment isn't expected until 2029-2030, and SK hynix is separately hiring 3D-stacked DRAM design engineers in the US.

@@REF@@[News] Samsung Reportedly Builds Hybrid Bonding Mass Production Line; Full-Scale Deployment Seen in 2029-2030 (TrendForce, 2026-07-22)|https://www.trendforce.com/news/2026/07/22/news-samsung-reportedly-builds-hybrid-bonding-mass-production-line-full-scale-deployment-seen-in-2029-2030/|https://img.trendforce.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/22144509/BESI-hybrid-bonding-tool-20260722-624x407.jpg

Taiwan's Winbond also gets named alongside CXMT in this niche, but its core business has traditionally been specialty memory: low-power DRAM and NOR flash for automotive and industrial customers. Its role in 3D IC is a newer addition, tied to a recent TSMC deal to supply DRAM for wafer-on-wafer stacking.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The question comes down to one thing: is skipping the niche 3D IC market a missed opportunity for Samsung and SK hynix, or just the right call for now.

If Samsung's Pyeongtaek line comes online on schedule in 2029-2030, the caution will have been a matter of timing. If CXMT or Winbond lock in 3D IC customers before then, this caution will go down as a missed window instead.
kobeissi-margin-debt-net-credit-record:
A fresh sign of investors piling into stocks with borrowed money rather than cash has emerged. According to The Kobeissi Letter, net credit balances (the cash investors hold in brokerage accounts minus margin debt) fell $70 billion in June to a record negative $1.06 trillion. Margin debt itself climbed $895 billion over the same period to a record $1.50 trillion.

## Checking the numbers first
FINRA's own raw data confirms these figures almost exactly. June 2026 margin debt came to $1.502 trillion, and combined free credit balances across cash and margin accounts came to $440.9 billion. Subtract one from the other and you get negative $1.061 trillion, matching Kobeissi's figure closely.

@@REF@@This $1.5 Trillion Bomb Is Waiting to Blow Up Your Portfolio (Yahoo Finance/24/7 Wall St, 2026-07-25)|https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/1-5-trillion-bomb-waiting-131609949.html

## But 'broad risk appetite' may only be half the story
Kobeissi contrasts this with 2008, when investors held more cash and net credit balances were positive. Other sources, though, put both the 2000 dot-com peak (-$130 billion) and the 2008 peak (-$60 billion) in negative territory, suggesting this comparison may be mixing different measurement methodologies. That discrepancy isn't fully resolved as of this writing.

The stronger evidence is about where the leverage is actually concentrated. Per Crypto Briefing, leveraged ETFs hold about $179 billion in total assets, and 85% of that sits in just three sectors: tech, AI and semiconductors. On June 5, a 3x leveraged semiconductor ETF fell 31% in a single session. In July, South Korea's Kospi dropped 27% after SK hynix said it would slow AI memory expansion, triggering margin calls across roughly 1.2 million Korean brokerage accounts, about 10% of all trading accounts in the country, that had bet on the sector through leveraged ETFs.

@@REF@@Korea's AI Stock Rout Is Becoming a Lesson in Leveraged Excess (Bloomberg, 2026-07-14)|https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-14/korea-s-ai-stock-rout-is-becoming-a-lesson-in-leveraged-excess

@@CMP@@Kobeissi's read|Investor risk appetite is at unprecedented levels.|What other sources suggest|The leverage isn't spread broadly, it's concentrated in AI and semiconductor leveraged ETFs and derivatives, and that structure has already blown up once, in Korea.
"Investors love risk across the board" and "leverage is stacked in one AI-shaped corner of the market" paint very different pictures of what happens in the next pullback.

## Has margin debt historically warned of corrections
Three prior episodes of margin debt surging more than 65%, March 2000 (dot-com), July 2007 (financial crisis) and October 2021 (2022 bear market), all preceded market tops by roughly two to six months. This is being counted as a fourth instance of the pattern. The sample size is only three or four cycles, though, and some analysts note debt and markets tend to rise together, making this more of a coincident indicator than a precise timing tool.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The question comes down to one thing: is a record-low net credit balance a warning for the whole market, or a risk concentrated in one AI/semiconductor-shaped corner of it.

If cracks show up first in sector-specific leveraged products, as they did in Korea, it's the latter. If a pullback spreads across the broader market, the former reading was right. Margin debt doesn't cause a decline, but once one starts, it can make it bigger.
jukan-korea-memory-mega-mou-950b:
SK hynix agreed to supply $750 billion (about 1,085 trillion won) worth of advanced memory chips to Nvidia and other US tech giants over the next five years. The same day, Samsung Electronics signed a separate memorandum of understanding with Broadcom covering $200 billion (about 290 trillion won) in memory supply and foundry cooperation, also over five years. Both were announced by Kim Yong-beom, South Korea's presidential chief of staff for policy, during President Lee Jae-myung's Silicon Valley trip, relayed by chip-industry commentator Jukan on X.

## Samsung's $200 billion with Broadcom checks out
Samsung's own newsroom release confirms this almost word for word: "more than $200 billion across memory and foundry" over five years. Fortune independently confirmed the same figure through its own reporting.

@@REF@@Samsung Electronics and Broadcom Expand Strategic Collaboration Across Memory and Foundry Technologies (Samsung Newsroom, 2026-07-25)|https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-and-broadcom-expand-strategic-collaboration-across-memory-and-foundry-technologies|https://img.global.news.samsung.com/global/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/25142854/Samsung-Semiconductors-Memory-and-Foundry-Technologies-Broadcom-MoU_Thumb932_F.jpg

## But SK hynix's $750 billion doesn't match Jensen Huang's own number
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said, the same day, in his own words: "SK Group and I are announcing today that our two companies will enter into business partnerships that will represent over $500 billion of business together." That $500 billion spans not just SK hynix's memory supply but SK Telecom's AI infrastructure, an investment in Naver, Hyundai robotics, LG, and an AI Frontier Lab, the whole SK Group conglomerate. The government's $750 billion figure appears to layer on additional pieces, including a separate SK hynix-Microsoft supply deal, under the broader "SK-Nvidia and others" framing. The two numbers are counting different things, so reading $750 billion as "the memory contract with Nvidia alone" overstates what's actually there.

@@REF@@Nvidia, SK to announce $500 billion partnership, Jensen Huang says (Korea Herald, 2026-07-25)|https://www.koreaherald.com/article/10819890|https://wimg.heraldcorp.com/news/cms/2026/07/25/news-p.v1.20260725.84bb149612514e73b1311fe2aa1af0c0_T1.jpg

## Even 'MOU or not' is contested
SK hynix's own newsroom release calls this a "Letter of Intent," meaning a framework requiring further negotiation, not a binding contract. But policy chief Kim Yong-beom pushed back directly on that framing in a Seoul Economic Daily interview, saying "this isn't simply a corporate MOU, expect quite large, meaningful numbers from investment attraction, strategic alliances, and long-term contracts." The people announcing the deal and the people drafting it are describing it differently.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/DDR5_SDRAM_%28with_scale%29_IMGP6298_smial_wp.jpg/960px-DDR5_SDRAM_%28with_scale%29_IMGP6298_smial_wp.jpg|A DRAM stick meant for a server slot. The core product in this deal is HBM4, bound for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform.|Wikimedia Commons|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:DDR5_SDRAM_(with_scale)_IMGP6298_smial_wp.jpg

The products involved are reasonably specific. The SK hynix-Nvidia side names HBM4 for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform; the Samsung-Broadcom side involves 2-nanometer-class foundry work and HBM4E. Around the same time, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei separately said the company had signed its own supply agreements with both Samsung and SK hynix, though no amount, product or duration was disclosed.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The question comes down to one thing: are these big announcements a real signal of order growth, or headline figures stretched as wide as possible to fit a presidential trip.

If Samsung and SK hynix confirm real order backlogs or contract progress with hard numbers in this week's Q2 earnings, that leans toward the former. If these are still sitting at "letter of intent" stage five years from now, this $950 billion figure will be the part of the announcement worth revisiting first.
jukan-apple-micron-china-memory-lobbying:
Apple is lobbying the White House to allow Chinese-made memory chips in its products, according to the Wall Street Journal. The chips in question come from Chinese DRAM maker CXMT and NAND maker YMTC. Micron, the US memory chipmaker, is reportedly pushing back hard, arguing the move should never be allowed. Chip-industry commentator Jukan, writing on X, disputed Apple's reasoning.

## This is a blacklist fight, not a tariff fight
The dispute is about export-control and national-security blacklists, not tariff exemptions. Two separate lists are in play: the Pentagon's "1260H list," which designates CXMT as a Chinese military-linked company, and Commerce's Entity List, which would effectively cut off US companies from doing business with CXMT if it's added. Apple is lobbying to keep CXMT off that list, not asking for a tariff discount.

## 'CXMT is cheap' is only half true
A July 26 comparison by Tom's Hardware found CXMT's 64GB DDR5 module priced about 2.2% below equivalent Samsung/SK hynix modules, despite a 40% larger die and worse yields. WCCFTech reported the same finding from Computex in June: "CXMT cheap is a myth, prices are almost on par with the big three." Apple's real motive for wanting CXMT appears to be supply, not price. While Samsung, SK hynix and Micron divert capacity toward AI-driven HBM, CXMT has no reason to make that pivot, leaving it with relatively more available inventory and flexible contract terms.

@@REF@@Chinese CXMT DRAM doesn't look like the budget savior many were expecting (Tom's Hardware, 2026-07-26)|https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/dram/chinese-cxmt-dram-doesnt-look-like-the-budget-savior-many-were-expecting-new-modules-enter-the-market-but-prices-still-track-the-big-three|https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/Y6RXNGdt5atPtqKHjD7EUW-1280-80.jpg

## The '$250 price hike' isn't a settled fact yet either
Jukan argued memory prices jumped roughly fivefold while raising Apple's per-unit cost by only $50, even as Apple raised iPhone prices by $250. Checking this, Apple hasn't actually raised iPhone prices yet. The real price increases announced June 25 hit Macs, iPads and Vision Pro: MacBook Air up $200, MacBook Pro up $500, Vision Pro up $500. The $250 figure is an IDC-style projection for the unreleased iPhone 18 Pro (estimates range $100-270, mostly clustered around $200), not a hike that's already happened. Separately, iPhone 17 prices did rise in Japan, but Forbes attributed that to a weak yen, not memory costs. The "$50 memory cost versus $250 iPhone hike" comparison mixes something that's already happened with something projected, and two different causes.

## The Micron-Apple grudge is real, though
One of Jukan's other claims holds up well. Reports sourced to the WSJ confirm Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra has a genuinely long-running tension with Apple, dating back to his time as a SanDisk co-founder in 1988, when he reportedly avoided meeting Apple representatives altogether. Mehrotra met directly with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick last week to oppose Apple's request, offering Micron's $250 billion US manufacturing investment through 2035 (Idaho, New York, Virginia) as the alternative.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The question comes down to one thing: is Apple's lobbying really about protecting consumers from price increases, or cover for securing supply.

If Apple wins approval for CXMT and YMTC and iPhone prices come down or hold steady, supply really was the goal. If prices go up anyway after approval, the "inflation protection" framing won't hold up.
semianalysis-amd-cuda-moat-advancing-ai-:
SemiAnalysis has raised AMD's odds of catching Nvidia from a flat 0% to what it now calls a great chance. It is a paid research shop that digs deep on semiconductors, and it has been especially hard on AMD's software. That such a shop changed its mind is the heart of this piece.
But it is worth reading why the same piece says it is still early.

## What changed its mind?
Two things drove the upgrade: the chip and the customers.
AMD's new MI455X accelerator is the first datacenter chip built on TSMC's 2-nanometer process.
It stacks HBM4 memory 12 high for 432 gigabytes per package, more than the 8 stacks and 288 gigabytes Nvidia and Google use.

@@CHK@@MI455X HBM4|432GB, 12 stacks|Nvidia & Google|288GB, 8 stacks|FP8 compute|20 petaflops@@On memory capacity and process node, AMD genuinely leads. The spec edge is real. But the two risks SemiAnalysis flags are about production and software, not specs, so these numbers alone don't settle it.@@Checked 2026-07-27 · AMD Advancing AI 2026 (2026-07-25) · NVIDIA public specs

The customers showed up too. Anthropic committed to 2 gigawatts of AMD chips, and AMD answered with an equity investment of up to 5 billion dollars in Anthropic.
Microsoft, which had dropped AMD after quality problems, reversed course and will bring the new racks into its cloud. The end user is expected to be OpenAI.

AMD's new Helios rack ties 72 GPUs into a single unit.|Wikimedia Commons|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tesla-NVIDIA_GPU_cluster_(3706444821).jpg

## So why only a 'chance'?
The headline and the body don't line up. That gap is the point of this card.

@@CMP@@What the headline says|From 0% to a great chance of success. AMD is finally challenging Nvidia's software moat.|What the same body says|Its key automated-test parity is still at 0%, and the 90% target was missed and pushed to October.

SemiAnalysis flags two risks.
One is rack production. Early Helios units hit reliability problems in the backplane, so the ramp is slow.
The other is heavier. AMD is chronically short of the in-house GPUs it needs to build and automatically test its software. SemiAnalysis writes that it has a single-digit multiple fewer than Nvidia.
With too little test hardware, the pass rate that shows whether the software is verified to Nvidia's level lags behind.

## Don't good specs settle it?
The same shop's own measurements from months ago point the other way.
In a February 2026 inference benchmark, SemiAnalysis said AMD's earlier chip was completely beaten by Nvidia's B200 on low-precision (FP4) disaggregated inference. On open-source distributed inference, it said AMD trailed by more than six months.
A spec-sheet lead and measured performance are still two different stories.

@@REF@@AMD to supply Anthropic with 2 gigawatts of Instinct MI450 GPUs (Tom's Hardware, 2026-07-22)|https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/amd-to-supply-anthropic-with-2-gigawatts-of-instinct-mi450-gpus|https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/iAtJT6Ab8gPu3iDZq9bCnL-1920-80.jpg

## How is this different from the last card?
If the Jukan card views the same CUDA-moat debate from the DeepSeek and Huawei side, this one views it from AMD's side.
Both say the software wall is getting lower. What is honest about this piece is that it stakes its conclusion on execution, not specs.
Adding memory and lining up customers is done. What is left is verifying the software that runs on top to Nvidia's level, and that won't be settled until after October.
meru-treasury-yield-deficit-not-just-oil: Rising oil prices explain only part of the Treasury yield spike, Korean investment blogger Meru argues, the bigger driver is a structural mismatch between how much debt Washington needs to sell and how much the market wants to buy. The 10-year yield broke above 4.7% intraday, and most coverage blames it on crude, since the Strait of Hormuz is blocked again and Houthi attacks threaten the Red Sea. Oil does feed into inflation broadly, through gasoline, plastics, fertilizer and power generation costs, but breakeven inflation, the rate implied by inflation-protected Treasuries, has barely moved, sitting around 2.3% for both 10 and 30-year debt. Instead, the 30-year real yield has climbed to its highest since the 2008 financial crisis, meaning borrowing itself has simply gotten more expensive. Meru traces that to Treasury supply and demand: the market has grown from $4.5 trillion in 2007 to $31 trillion today, China has flipped from buyer to net seller in favor of gold, Japanese investors sold $29.6 billion of Treasuries net in Q1 2026, and the Fed keeps shrinking its balance sheet. Washington's annual interest bill has topped $1.2 trillion, the FY2026 deficit is projected near $2.07 trillion, and a Supreme Court ruling against IEEPA tariffs forced billions in refunds that analysts say adds roughly $180 billion a year to the deficit through 2036. Big Tech is competing for the same buyers too: global corporate bond issuance hit a record $3.68 trillion in the first half of 2026, led by Amazon's $54 billion, forcing the Treasury to offer richer yields to compete for pension and insurance money.
serenity-aaoi-pluggables-cpo-coexist:
The debate over whether co-packaged optics (CPO) will soon make traditional pluggable optical transceivers obsolete in AI data centers got a reality check this week. Analyst Serenity relayed comments from a photonics-industry CEO, made on a podcast, arguing pluggables have roughly another decade of relevant commercial life left, not months.

## Who is this CEO, actually
It turns out the comment didn't come from an AAOI executive at all. It came from Vickram Vathulya, CEO of Sivers Semiconductors, a Swedish company that makes continuous-wave (CW) lasers. The podcast was Laser Focus World's "Expert Insights: Photonics & AI," aired July 21, with Oriole CEO James Regan also on the call. Sivers sells laser components into both CPO and pluggable supply chains, worth noting since it has little to lose either way this debate resolves.

The exchange started with a reader asking whether Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) is in trouble as CPO gains traction. Serenity's answer: not exactly. AAOI is also developing CPO technology, just further behind on commercializing it than some peers.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Tesla-NVIDIA_GPU_cluster_%283706444821%29.jpg/960px-Tesla-NVIDIA_GPU_cluster_%283706444821%29.jpg|A rack of GPUs in an AI data center. The optical cabling that links racks like this is what's actually being argued over.|Wikimedia Commons|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tesla-NVIDIA_GPU_cluster_(3706444821).jpg

## The claim mostly checks out anyway
Independent of Vathulya's framing, real industry data leans toward pushing back on the idea that CPO is about to take over. SemiAnalysis, in a June report, pushed full CPO mass production out to 2028-2029, citing yield math: a single optical engine might yield 95%, but with 32 engines per switch, system-level yield drops to around 19%.

@@REF@@Lumentum and the Laser Bottleneck (Chipstrat, 2026-03-02)|https://www.chipstrat.com/p/lumentum-and-the-laser-bottleneck

Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston has said the company is "undershipping our customers' demand by somewhere around 30%." Nvidia locked in $2 billion each with Lumentum and Coherent in March, $4 billion total, to secure priority laser supply.

@@REF@@AI Data Center Optical Component Shortage: Nvidia's $4B Laser Lockup Pushes Rivals Past 2027 (Tech Times, 2026-05-27)|https://www.techtimes.com/articles/317281/20260527/ai-data-center-optical-component-shortage-nvidias-4b-laser-lockup-pushes-rivals-past-2027.htm

AAOI itself confirmed on its May earnings call that an industry-wide indium phosphide laser shortage is likely to persist, and said it plans to expand its own laser capacity by 350% by 2027.

## A third option: near-package optics
The CEO's bigger point, as relayed, is that the industry is heading toward several coexisting architectures rather than one clean winner. Besides pluggables and CPO, there's a newer category called near-package optics (NPO), which sits closer to the chip than a pluggable without going as far as full co-packaging. Component makers including Credo, Marvell, Coherent and Lumentum are confirmed to be building in this space. It's less clear whether Nvidia or Broadcom use the NPO label in their own switch roadmaps, which suggests NPO is more a component-supplier category riding alongside the CPO platforms than a named hyperscaler initiative.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The question comes down to one thing: if pluggables, CPO and NPO all coexist for a decade, which optical suppliers actually win.

What holds back all three paths isn't which architecture wins, it's laser and raw-material supply. The longer CPO slips, the longer pluggables stay relevant, and the bigger NPO's window gets too. This is secondhand color from a podcast relayed through a tweet, but its direction lines up with what the industry data actually shows.
kobeissi-m2-outpaces-gdp-g7: Money creation keeps outpacing real economic growth across the G7, a fresh set of figures shows. According to The Kobeissi Letter, Canada's M2 money supply (a measure of cash, checking deposits and savings-type accounts) has grown 368% since January 2004, the largest increase among G7 economies, while the Canadian economy expanded just 159% in nominal terms over the same period. The US shows a similar gap, with M2 up 279% against 171% nominal GDP growth. France's M2 has surged 258% and the eurozone's 211%, both far outpacing nominal growth of 84% and 102% respectively. Japan is the outlier in the other direction, with M2 up only 90% since 2004, but its economy grew just 25% over that span, the slowest pace in the G7. Kobeissi frames this as a widening gap between how fast money is being created and how fast economies are actually growing.
trump-xi-putin-no-weapons-iran: President Trump said both Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin personally assured him they will not sell weapons to Iran, a claim that, if it holds, would cut off two of the countries most capable of arming Tehran as its war grinds into its fifth month. Trump wrote on Truth Social that Xi made the pledge at their recent meeting in Beijing and said it extends to Chinese companies as well, not just the government. He framed the assurance as tied to the broader US-China relationship, saying he is doing Xi "very big favors" in return. On Putin, Trump said the Russian leader made a similar commitment despite the ongoing war in Ukraine, where Russia's relationship with the US continues alongside its ties to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Trump drew a distinction with his own weapons sales, saying the US sells arms to NATO countries rather than directly to Ukraine, and that what those countries do with the weapons afterward is not something he tracks. He added that any weapons flow from China or Russia to Iran would be "very bad for them," without elaborating on what response that might trigger. The statement comes as Iran has already rejected a US-backed ceasefire proposal from Iraqi mediators, and as oil and shipping routes near the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea remain under pressure from the conflict. Neither Beijing nor Moscow has publicly confirmed Trump's account of the conversations.
jukan-amd-mi500-tam-14t: Semiconductor analyst Jeff Pu has raised his forecast for the AI accelerator market to $1.4 trillion by 2030, up from an earlier $1 trillion estimate, and now expects the market to already reach $1 trillion by 2028, according to a note relayed by chip-industry commentator Jukan on X. Pu's note, focused on AMD's AI roadmap, also lifted the server CPU total addressable market to more than $220 billion by 2030, with agentic AI workloads expected to make up roughly half of that demand and the ratio of CPUs to GPUs in data centers tightening toward 1:1. On AMD's own hardware, Pu highlighted the MI455X accelerator as a major step up from its predecessor, the MI355X, citing 34 times higher throughput and 18 times lower cost per generated token, and said it already beats Nvidia's B200 chip on some large language model inference workloads. Looking further out, Pu said AMD's next-generation MI500 chip will bring optical interconnects, a faster way of linking chips together using light instead of electrical signals, putting it ahead of Nvidia's upcoming Rubin Ultra chip in areas like high-bandwidth memory, four-die packaging, and how many chips can be linked into a single system. He also flagged AMD's Venice server CPU as the strongest option for AI workloads, with 2 to 2.2 times higher throughput than competing chips, and estimated around 300,000 CoWoS advanced packaging units will be built for AMD in 2027, which would lift the average price AMD can charge per chip. Pu kept his price target and estimates unchanged despite the upgraded market forecasts.
kobeissi-equity-etf-record-880b: US equity ETFs have pulled in $880 billion in new money so far this year, already the second-largest annual haul on record after only the all-time high set in 2025, and on pace to blow past that record before year-end, according to data highlighted by The Kobeissi Letter. The current pace of inflows is more than double what the market saw at the same point in both 2021 and 2025, two years that themselves ranked among the strongest on record for equity fund flows. If inflows keep coming in at this rate, Kobeissi estimates the full-year total could top $1.4 trillion, roughly $500 billion above the roughly $920 billion record set in 2025. The scale of buying stands out given how choppy the past week has been for stocks. The S&P 500 gave back a full day's gains and closed lower on Thursday as the Iran war escalated, and Intel's post-earnings rally evaporated within days, wiping out about $90 billion in market value. Investors pulling back from individual stocks or single-day swings evidently haven't pulled back from US equities as an asset class overall, at least not yet. Whether that gap between headline-driven day-to-day selling and steady underlying inflows can keep holding as the Iran conflict grinds into its fifth month is an open question the market hasn't had to answer yet.
kobeissi-intel-erases-rally: Intel's stock has erased its entire post-earnings rally, falling 4% on Thursday after surging as much as 15% following Tuesday's blowout second-quarter report, The Kobeissi Letter reports. The reversal has wiped out roughly $90 billion in market capitalization since the rally peaked around 4:20 p.m. ET the day after earnings. Intel had posted its strongest quarterly revenue growth in more than fifteen years on Tuesday, with the Data Center and AI segment up 59% to $6.3 billion, sending shares up double digits in the days that followed. But the gains proved short-lived. The pullback comes as broader market volatility rose Thursday, with the S&P 500 also giving back its gains as the Iran war escalated and technology stocks fell across the board, muddying the read on whether Intel's retreat reflects specific doubts about the earnings quality or simply a risk-off day for the whole market. Intel's GAAP results still showed an $11 billion net loss driven by one-time charges even as adjusted profit swung positive, a split that some investors may be revisiting now that the initial excitement has faded. The stock remains up from where it started the week, but the speed of the reversal shows how quickly gains tied to a single earnings beat can unwind once the market has time to sit with the details.
kobeissi-sp500-iran-war-selloff: The S&P 500 gave back its entire daily gain and closed lower on Thursday, as an escalation in the Iran war triggered a broad pullback in technology stocks, The Kobeissi Letter reports. The index had been trading in positive territory earlier in the session before reversing course, a move Kobeissi tied directly to the intensifying conflict, now in its 145th day after Iran rejected a US-brokered ceasefire proposal put forward by Iraqi mediators. The reversal landed on a day already crowded with unsettling cross-currents for markets. Intel's post-earnings rally evaporated, wiping out roughly $90 billion in market value, and the 30-day correlation between AI infrastructure stocks and the semiconductor index had separately collapsed toward zero, the lowest in more than four and a half years. Taken together, the day's price action suggests investors are growing more selective and more nervous at the same time, willing to sell first and ask questions later when geopolitical risk resurfaces, even against a backdrop of record equity ETF inflows earlier in the year. Oil and Treasury markets have already been carrying a war-risk premium for months, and a longer, more uncertain conflict raises the odds that equity markets start pricing in the same risk more persistently, rather than treating each escalation as a one-day scare.
serenity-googl-waymo-uber-split: Uber and Google's self-driving unit Waymo may be headed for a split, the Financial Times reported, according to investor commentary account Serenity, who says the shift confirms a view held for over a year. Serenity had argued that Uber's partnership with Waymo was a mistake from the start, since it effectively turned Uber into a distribution channel Google could use to scale its own robotaxi service before eventually competing directly. In Serenity's view, that risk has essentially been realized: Waymo, now positioned as Uber's own partner, looks set to become one of its most serious disruptors in ride-hailing. Serenity had previously flagged that other neutral players, such as Nebius's Avride, or a fully vertically integrated approach, would have made more sense for Uber's long-term positioning than tying its distribution to a company with its own robotaxi ambitions. The report adds a new wrinkle to how investors read Alphabet's self-driving bet: rather than a side project, Waymo increasingly looks like a business Alphabet could operate on its own terms, independent of the ride-hailing incumbents it once needed for scale. For Uber, the question shifts from whether Waymo helps fill its network to whether Waymo eventually competes with it directly for the same riders.
kobeissi-datacenter-power-2035: US data center electricity demand is projected to jump 253% from 2026 levels to a record 194 gigawatts by 2035, The Kobeissi Letter reports, a figure roughly equal to the output of 194 traditional nuclear reactors. As a result, data centers are expected to account for about 20% of total US electricity consumption by 2035, up from roughly 6% today, with the share already projected to hit 12% by 2030. Much of the buildout is concentrated in a handful of grid regions, chief among them PJM, the interconnection that serves Washington DC and 13 states including Virginia, Pennsylvania and Ohio, where AI data center clusters are expanding fastest. The projection captures a shift already visible in utility earnings and grid planning: power availability, not chip supply, is increasingly the constraint that determines how fast hyperscalers can bring new AI capacity online. Utilities in PJM territory have flagged multiyear queues for new large-load interconnections, and grid operators warn that demand growth of this scale requires new generation and transmission capacity, and in some cases, direct on-site power deals that bypass the public grid entirely.
trump-eu-301-investigation-bigtech-fines: President Trump announced the US has opened a Section 301 investigation into what he calls the European Union's practice of "robbing" American companies through antitrust fines, and threatened a "substantial tariff" on the EU in response. In a Truth Social post, Trump listed the EU's recent penalties: $15 billion against Apple, $3 billion against Meta, $2.5 billion against Amazon, and, just announced, another $1 billion against Google, which he said brings Google's cumulative EU fines above $18 billion. He called the fines "illegal and highly discriminatory," said they began under the Biden administration, and pledged the practice "is not going to continue during the Trump Administration." Section 301 is a US trade law tool that lets the president investigate a foreign government's practices and, if found unfair, impose retaliatory tariffs without new legislation, the same authority Trump has used against China and other trading partners. He gave no specific tariff rate or timeline, saying only that penalties on US companies "will be entirely reversed" and a tariff is expected "at the earliest possible moment." The EU has used antitrust enforcement against US tech giants for years under its Digital Markets Act and general competition rules, arguing the fines address anticompetitive conduct rather than target American firms specifically.
jensen-open-models-letter: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang posted on X for the first time on July 24th, using the debut to share a letter Nvidia signed arguing that open AI models deserve as much support as closed, proprietary ones. The letter states that AI will transform every industry, power every company, and eventually be built by every country, and argues open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, speed up innovation and its spread to more users, and let countries build AI systems under their own control rather than depending entirely on foreign providers. Huang's post frames the choice between open and closed models as false, saying the world needs both kinds of frontier systems rather than picking one over the other. The full letter is posted as a PDF on Nvidia's own site. Huang's move comes as Nvidia, whose GPUs power most AI training and inference worldwide, has increasingly positioned itself as a backer of open-weight models such as Meta's Llama family, even as it also profits from closed labs like OpenAI and Anthropic buying its chips. Taking a public stance now lands in the middle of an active policy fight in Washington and Beijing over whether open-source AI helps or threatens national security, a debate that could shape future export rules and government AI contracts.
kobeissi-ai-capex-sox-correlation-collap: The stock market is starting to treat AI chipmakers and AI spenders as two separate trades instead of one, The Kobeissi Letter reports. The 30-day correlation between the largest US capital-expenditure spenders on AI infrastructure and the semiconductor index, the SOX, has fallen to near zero, the lowest reading in at least four and a half years. That's down sharply from +0.78 in April, and well below the +0.60 average correlation since the start of 2022. Since early June the two groups have moved in opposite directions: semiconductor stocks have rallied even as the biggest AI infrastructure spenders, the hyperscalers pouring hundreds of billions into data centers, have declined, and the pattern has also run in reverse on other days. Kobeissi reads the split as a sign that investors no longer see AI chip demand and AI infrastructure spending as a single story that rises and falls together. Chipmakers keep benefiting from AI demand regardless of who is paying for it, while hyperscalers face growing questions about whether their spending will generate enough revenue to justify the cost. Kobeissi's conclusion is that the next phase of the AI trade will be judged on profitability rather than on how much companies are willing to spend.
netinterest-stripe-paypal-bid: Stripe and private equity firm Advent have offered to acquire PayPal for around $53 billion, Net Interest's Marc Rubinstein reports, with the deal reportedly structured so Stripe and Advent would each own half of PayPal, backed by $50 billion in committed bank financing. The offer follows a secondary tender offer that valued Stripe itself at $159 billion, and it closes a loop that started in 2013, when PayPal, then still owned by eBay, tried to buy Stripe outright and was turned down by founders Patrick and John Collison. PayPal instead bought Braintree, the maker of Venmo, for $800 million, but over the following decade Stripe's payment volume compounded at 70% a year against Braintree's 43%. Last year Stripe processed $1.9 trillion in payments to Braintree's $600 billion. PayPal, meanwhile, has churned through three CEOs in three years and a string of missteps since. Rubinstein frames the central question as why Stripe, now the clear winner of that old rivalry, wants to buy the company it once tried to escape, and whether $53 billion is close to the right price, a question his fuller analysis addresses beyond this preview.
